title: the Buddha's past lives as animals
hook: the Buddha's past lives as animals; the monkey king
carry: the bridge he made of his body

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sangha, the community, the third jewel. Your line was you need people. Today, a story. Day eighteen.

A huge mango tree grows on the bank of a river. In it lives a troop of monkeys, eighty thousand of them, the story says, and their king. One night a human king's archers surround the tree. They mean to shoot every monkey at dawn. There's no way down. The monkeys are trapped between the arrows and the river. And the monkey king looks across the water at the far bank, and makes a decision. This is one of hundreds of stories Buddhists have told children, and grown-ups, for many centuries. The monkey king, they say, was the Buddha.
screen: `A MANGO TREE BY A RIVER.` → `ARCHERS WAITING FOR DAWN.` → `THE MONKEY KING DECIDES.`

segments.voice: The Jataka. The word means birth stories. They're tales of the Buddha's earlier lives, before he became the Buddha, when he was still on the long way. Buddhist tradition says he lived countless lives, as kings and merchants and poor men, and very often as animals: a hare, a deer, an elephant, a quail, a monkey. The Pali collection has around five hundred and fifty of them, and Jataka scenes are carved in stone on some of the oldest Buddhist monuments in India. Here's the monkey king's story, the way it's told. He leaps across the river to the far bank and ties one end of a long cane to a tree. He ties the other end around his own waist and leaps back. But the cane is too short. He can reach the mango tree only with his hands. So he grips a branch and stretches his body out across the gap. And he tells his monkeys: cross. One by one, all of them run across the cane, and over his back, to safety. His body is torn by it. The human king has watched the whole thing from below. He's so moved that he has the monkey king gently brought down and cared for. And before he dies, the monkey king teaches him what a ruler is for: a king should care for his people the way I cared for mine. Each Jataka ends by telling you who was who, and in this one the monkey king was the future Buddha. Why tell stories like this? Because they show the path from the inside. Generosity. Courage. Compassion. Not as ideas, but as a monkey holding on to a branch until the last one is across.
screen: `JATAKA — BIRTH STORIES.` · `HARE, DEER, ELEPHANT, MONKEY.` · `THE CANE TOO SHORT.` · `A KING LEARNS WHAT RULING IS FOR.` · then, large: `THE BRIDGE HE MADE OF HIS BODY.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Feel your own arms and shoulders, the part of you that would do the holding. Now bring to mind someone trying to get across something right now: a kid with an exam, a friend in a hard month, a coworker drowning in a deadline. Not a grand rescue. Just one small stretch that could help: staying late, holding the door a little longer, listening to the end of the story. Picture holding on while they cross. Notice what it costs, and what it gives.
The Jataka. Birth stories: the Buddha's past lives, many as animals, showing the path from the inside. Eighteenth word.
Your line: the bridge he made of his body. Small stretches count too. That's day eighteen.

howItsDone: Buddhists tell the Jataka stories to children, perform them in dance and drama, paint them on temple walls, and hear them in sermons; in Theravada countries the last ten Jatakas are especially loved, and the Vessantara Jataka is staged at festivals.

fork.setup: you're the monkey king. you've tied a cane across the river, but it's too short to reach the tree. your troop is trapped. what do you do?

hold the branch and make your body the last part of the bridge.

fork.reveal: he grips the branch and stretches across the gap, and every monkey runs over his back to safety. the watching king is so moved he cares for him.

what it means: stories of the Buddha's earlier lives, many as animals, that show the path's virtues in action.
what a scholar hears: the Jātaka collection of about 547 tales; the monkey king is the Mahākapi Jātaka (no. 407). Jataka scenes appear in stone at Bharhut and Sanchi.
